paragraphs.text: [calm] True! — nervous — very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am. But why do you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses. It had dulled none of them. Above all, my hearing had become acute. I heard everything in heaven and on earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad? Hearken! See how calmly I can tell you the whole story.

It is impossible to say how the idea first entered my head. But once it had entered, it haunted me day and night. I loved the old man. He had never wronged me. He had never insulted me. I had no desire for his gold. I think it was his eye — yes, it was this! He had the eye of a vulture — a pale blue eye, with a film over it. Whenever it fell upon me, my blood ran cold. Little by little, I made up my mind to kill the old man and rid myself of that eye forever.

[nervous] You should have seen how wisely I went about it — with what caution, what foresight, what dissimulation! I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I killed him. Every night, about midnight, I turned the latch of his door and opened it — oh, so gently! When there was room for my head, I put in a lantern, closed, closed, so that no light shone out. Then I put in my head. It took me an hour to get my whole head inside and see him on the bed. Would a madman have been so wise?

Once my head was inside, I opened the lantern just enough for a single thin ray to fall on his eye. For seven nights — every night at midnight — I looked in on him as he slept. But the eye was always closed, and so I could not do it. His Evil Eye alone vexed me. I had nothing against the old man himself. Every morning I greeted him warmly by name and asked how he had slept.

On the eighth night I was more cautious than ever. The minute hand of a watch moved faster than my hand on the door. Never before had I felt so sure of my own powers — my sagacity. I could scarcely contain my triumph. To think that I was opening his door little by little and he had no idea what I was doing! I chuckled, and perhaps he heard me, for he stirred in bed. The shutters were fastened and the room was pitch-dark. He could not see the door move, so I kept pushing it open. I had my head inside and was about to open the lantern when my thumb slipped on the metal fastening. The old man sat up in bed. "Who's there?" he cried.

[whispers] For a whole hour I stood still, without a word. I never heard him lie down. Then came a quiet groan. I knew it for the sound of terror. I had made that sound myself often enough, listening to noises in the wall at midnight. I pitied him, though I laughed to myself. I imagined him telling himself it was only the wind, or a mouse crossing the floor. Still he listened. Death's shadow had reached him. He could neither see nor hear me, yet he felt I was there. At last I opened a little — a very, very little crevice in the lantern. A ray as thin as a spider's thread fell straight on the vulture eye. It was open — wide, wide open. Fury seized me. I could see only that dull blue eye, with its hideous veil. The rest of his face was lost in darkness.

And have I not told you that you mistake the sharpness of my senses for madness? Now, I say, I heard a low, dull, quick sound, like a watch wrapped in cotton. I knew that sound well. It was the beating of the old man's heart. It drove me into a fury. But I kept still. I scarcely breathed. I held the lantern steady as the beating grew quicker and louder. In the silence of that house, the sound began to terrify me. For several more minutes I stood there. Louder, louder! I thought the heart would burst. Then a new fear seized me. What if a neighbor heard it through the wall?

[gasp] I flung the lantern open and leaped into the room with a yell. The old man shrieked once. I dragged him to the floor and pulled the heavy bed over him. I smiled, sure that the worst was over. For minutes I could still hear the muffled beating. Then it stopped. I pulled the bed away. I laid my hand on his chest and felt no pulse. He was dead. His eye would trouble me no more. I dismembered the body and hid it beneath three floorboards. I replaced the planks so neatly that no human eye — not even his — could have seen anything wrong.

About four o'clock in the morning, a knock sounded at the door. Three police officers had come to search the house. A neighbor had reported a shriek in the night. I smiled. What had I to fear? I told them I had cried out in a dream and that the old man was away in the country. I led them through the house and urged them to search every room. In his bedroom I showed them that all his valuables were untouched.

[sigh] I brought chairs into the room and invited the officers to rest. I set my own chair directly over the spot where the body lay and sat down. The officers seemed satisfied. They chatted about ordinary things and I answered cheerfully. Before long I felt myself growing pale. My head ached, and I thought I heard a ringing in my ears. I talked louder to drown it out. The sound grew clearer and clearer, until it seemed to come from somewhere beyond my ears. It was that low, dull, quick sound again, like a watch wrapped in cotton.

[nervous] I jumped up and argued about trifles, raising my voice and waving my arms. Yet the sound kept growing louder. Why would they not go? I paced the floor. I foamed — I raved — I swore! I scraped my chair across the boards, but even that could not drown it out. Still the officers chatted and smiled. Was it possible they could not hear it? Almighty God — no, no! They heard — they suspected — they knew! They were making a mockery of my horror. I thought so then, and I think so now.

[tense silence] I could bear those smiles no longer. I had to scream or die. And now — again — hark! Louder! Louder! Louder! "Villains!" I shrieked. "Dissemble no more! I admit the deed! Tear up the planks — here, here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!"

quizzes.question: What does the narrator think first made him want to kill the old man?
options: The old man's pale, clouded eye frightened him.
The old man had stolen his money.
The old man insulted him in front of others.

quizzes.question: How does the sound seem to change while the officers chat?
options: At first it seems to come from the officers' conversation, then from the street.
At first it seems to ring in his ears, then it seems to come from outside them.
At first it reminds him of a ticking watch, then it seems to ring in his ears.
